messages.content: Get me this coming Saturday's weather forecast?

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

message.content: Sure! To give you an accurate forecast for the upcoming Saturday (June 27, 2026), could you let me know which city or region you'd like the weather for? If you prefer, I can also ask for your latitude and longitude directly.

The user wants the weather forecast for "this coming Saturday". We need to interpret "this coming Saturday" as the next upcoming Saturday relative to today. Today is 2026-06-25. Let's check what day of week that is. 2026-06-25 is a Thursday? Let's quickly compute: 2026-06-25. I can approximate: 2026-01-01 is a Monday? Actually let's just use known reference: 2023-01-01 was a Sunday. 2026-01-01 would be 3 years later, including leap year 2024. So 2023-01-01 Sunday + 365 days (2023) -> 2024-01-01 Monday? Wait 2023-01-01 Sunday. 2023 has 365 days, so 2024-01-01 is Monday. 2024 is leap year, 366 days, so 2025-01-01 is Wednesday? Actually 2024-01-01 Monday + 366 days mod 7 = 2 days shift, so 2025-01-01 Wednesday. 2025 has 365 days, so 2026-01-01 is Thursday. So 2026-01-01 Thursday. Now we need 2026-06-25. From Jan 1 to June 25 inclusive? Let's count days: Jan 31, Feb 28 (2026 not leap), Mar 31, Apr 30, May 31, Jun 25. Sum: 31+28+31+30+31+25 = 176 days. Starting on Thursday, add 175 days (since Jan 1 is day 1). 175 mod 7 = 175 - 7*25=175-175=0. So same weekday: Thursday. So 2026-06-25 is Thursday. Good.

So "this coming Saturday" would be the next Saturday after Thursday 2026-06-25. That would be 2026-06-27 (Saturday). So we need forecast for 2026-06-27. We need to get weather forecast from Open-Meteo API. We need coordinates. The user didn't specify location. We might ask for location. But maybe we can assume some default location? The user didn't provide location. We could ask clarifying question. But the instruction says: "If you do not have enough information to answer the user's query, ask clarifying questions." So we should ask for location. Also we might ask for time zone? But we can just ask for location. So we respond asking for location.
